newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia eyes 15 percent consumption tax - paper.
newsitem.headline: Australia eyes 15 percent consumption tax - paper.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello, cranking up the government's campaign for tax reform, has told fellow parliamentarians he wanted a goods and services tax (GST) rate of at least 15 percent, The Australian newspaper reported on Wednesday.

It said Costello told a private meeting of Liberal/National parliamentarians on Monday night a GST rate of at least 15 percent was needed to abolish current sales taxes and fund necessary income tax cuts.
It was the government's most specific reference to a GST widely seen at the centre of a tax reform package likely to be proposed at the next election.
The mooted 15-percent rate compares with the GST rate of 12.5 percent in neighbouring New Zealand and the 17.5-percent rate of Value-Added Tax (VAT) in Britain.

"Coalition backbenchers said the cost of abolishing sales tax would be a GST rate equivalent to around six percent, with another three to four percent for removing petrol excise and an additional three percent to remove state payroll taxes," The Australian said.
"Income tax cuts of more than A$5 billion (US$3.75 billion) would need a GST rate of at least two percent," the newspaper said. The combined amount proposed by Costello would be at least 15 percent.

Costello also told the meeting that unless tax reform was done urgently, the government would face a political problem with people earning average weekly earnings being hit by the top marginal tax rate for the first time, The Australian said.
The top rate of tax, at 47 percent, kicks in at an annual salary of A$50,000.
The government is widely expected to propose some form of consumption tax or GST in the next election campaign scheduled for early 1999.
The coalition -- which lost what was regarded as an easy-win election in 1993 with a GST policy -- pledged in the 1996 election not to introduce a consumption tax in its first three-year term.
But a series of recent opinion polls have showed growing community support for a GST and Prime Minister John Howard has not ruled out its introduction in the second term of government.
Howard said earlier this month that tax reforms would boost economic growth and employment and Costello has said a mulit-stage value-added tax should be considered.
